title: Ronald Hutton Publishes The Witch: A History of Fear
description:
Ronald Hutton's The Witch: A History of Fear, from Ancient Times to the Present, published by Yale University Press in 2017 (the entry date of 2004 should refer to an earlier publication; the main work appeared in 2017 — this entry records Hutton's ongoing contribution beginning with earlier works), represents the culmination of Hutton's decades-long engagement with the history of witch beliefs and the social history of magic in Britain. Hutton, a social and cultural historian at the University of Bristol, approaches witchcraft from a perspective that emphasizes the diversity of folk practitioners, the social function of magical beliefs, and the need to understand witch prosecution within specific regional and temporal contexts. His work consistently challenges both the Murray thesis of ancient fertility cult survival and any monocausal account of the witch hunts.

Hutton's contribution to witchcraft studies builds on his earlier works: The Pagan Religions of the Ancient British Isles (1991), The Triumph of the Moon: A History of Modern Pagan Witchcraft (1999), and Shamans: Siberian Spirituality and the Western Imagination (2001). Across these works, Hutton developed a distinctive approach that combined rigorous archival scholarship with sensitivity to the perspective of practitioners — both historical and contemporary — and a commitment to distinguishing historical evidence from romantic reconstruction. His demolition of the Murray thesis in The Triumph of the Moon was thorough and definitive, conducted without polemic but with systematic attention to what the evidence actually showed.

The Witch (2017) synthesized Hutton's career-long engagement with global perspectives on witch-belief, tracing the elements of the European witch concept through comparative anthropology, classical antiquity, and diverse cultural contexts to argue that the specific synthesis that produced prosecuted witchcraft was a historically specific European construction rather than a universal feature of human belief. The book challenges both the universalism implicit in some anthropological approaches and the European exceptionalism in some historical accounts.
historiographical_note: Hutton's work represents the definitive social-historical account of witchcraft studies, complementing Clark's intellectual history and Ginzburg's microhistory as one of the three foundational scholarly traditions for this project. His demolition of the Murray thesis is universally accepted by specialists. His comparative approach in The Witch has been engaged by anthropologists and historians of religion as well as historians of early modern Europe. The WitchcraftStudiesDB treats Hutton alongside Clark and Ginzburg as a defining methodological tradition.
source_method: Primary scholarship (Hutton, The Witch, 2017; The Triumph of the Moon, 1999); subsequent scholarly responses
